title: 'Can I Do It Again': Harshal Patel Eyes New Ball in Ranji Reboot With Gujarat
excerpt: After 15 years with Haryana, the 35-year-old seamer wants the new ball for Gujarat — and says red-ball grind is the secret behind his white-ball success.
body:
• Harshal Patel, 35, will turn out for Gujarat in the Ranji Trophy 2026 season after 15 years with Haryana — and the IPL's 2021 Purple Cap winner wants to bowl with the new ball in red-ball cricket.
  • “The central question for me, as long as I keep playing cricket, is: can I do it again?” Patel told Cricinfo, describing the drive to keep proving himself as the force behind his late-career reinvention.
  • Patel credits red-ball cricket for his white-ball success: “If I look back at all my successful seasons, whether in white-ball cricket or the IPL, they've always come on the back of a really good red-ball season.”
  • He also offered a contrarian take on load management — not saving the body, but stressing it enough to adapt: “A lot of people misunderstand load management. They think it means saving your body… I look at it as giving your body enough stress and allowing your body enough time to adapt.”

At 35, with an IPL Purple Cap and an India career behind him, Harshal Patel is starting over. The seamer has moved to Gujarat after a decade and a half with Haryana, and ahead of his first Ranji Trophy game for his new state, he has set himself an unfamiliar challenge: bowling with the new ball in first-class cricket.

“What you can do over four days of cricket, or over a 20-over spell in a day, no other format allows you to do,” Patel told Cricinfo. “The more I bowl and play in competitive environments, the better my game gets.”

Red ball as the engine room

Patel's career has been built on a counterintuitive belief: that the grind of long-form cricket is what sharpens a white-ball specialist. “If I look back at all my successful seasons, whether in white-ball cricket or the IPL, they've always come on the back of a really good red-ball season,” he said. “I know that if I grind through red-ball cricket and get my skills really tight and solid, that will translate into what is my bread and butter.”

That philosophy powered his 2021 breakthrough, when he took 32 wickets for Royal Challengers Bengaluru to win the IPL Purple Cap — equalling the all-time record for a single season — and earned his India debut against New Zealand later that year. Now he wants the new ball, the sternest test of a seamer's craft, as the next proving ground.

“Can I do it again?”

What keeps a 35-year-old fast bowler grinding through Ranji Trophy mornings? Patel's answer is disarmingly simple.

“The central question for me, as long as I keep playing cricket, is: can I do it again? That's the only thing that pushes me to do whatever I have to do to compete.”

— Harshal Patel, to Cricinfo

It is a philosophy of deliberate discomfort. “You can go and slog for two hours in the nets every day, but it's nowhere near the intensity of competition,” he said. “It's about putting myself in situations where I can bowl a lot of overs in competition, make an impact for the team and win games.”

A different view of load management

Patel, who takes a keen interest in strength and conditioning principles, also pushed back on the modern orthodoxy around workload. “A lot of people misunderstand load management. They think it means saving your body for the rigours of long-form cricket, but I look at it as giving your body enough stress and allowing your body enough time to adapt, so that whatever you face during the season doesn't come as a shock,” he said.

That means diligence with strength work, recovery and load building — not avoidance of it. For a bowler whose variations made him one of the IPL's most reliable death bowlers, the red-ball reset with Gujarat is the latest application of a career-long method: get uncomfortable, get sharp, then go again.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora's weekend cricketers and armchair analysts, Patel's story is the rare late-career reinvention tale — proof that the domestic grind still matters in the franchise era, and that a bowler written off as a T20 specialist can still chase the new ball at 35.

What's next

The Ranji Trophy season will show whether Patel's red-ball-first formula still works in a new dressing room — and whether the new ball, in unfamiliar hands, becomes the weapon that extends one of Indian domestic cricket's most unusual careers.
